prospect.name: Nate Slayton
prospect.occupation: Marketing director, fully remote — "I don't go to an office, just sit down all day" — and describes the role as very stressful.
prospect.family_status: Two children, aged four and one; second child born about a year ago
prospect.training_background: Two strength sessions a week of about 35 minutes at the gym, plus yoga roughly once a week. Was training three days a week regularly before the second baby, with some running that the knee has since ruled out. Has done kettlebell training before and keeps two kettlebells in his home office, but is self-taught and does not trust his own form. Has previously worked with an online trainer and valued the accountability. Has tracked macros in the past with good results but does not want to again.
prospect.medical: Osgood-Schlatter disease diagnosed at 14, now requiring surgery to remove a bone fragment attached to the patellar tendon. Diagnosed by an orthopedic surgeon two days before the call; MRI booked for Thursday 9 July at 2pm Eastern, surgeon follow-up Monday 13 July, and he expects four to six weeks on crutches afterwards. Cannot run; squats and gym movement are tolerated but painful. Chronic lower-back tightness and pain that has never been formally diagnosed, worse after strength training and with no stretching, plus mild hip stiffness that has worsened over the past year. Taking Lexapro, an SSRI, for anxiety; associates it with a 7 lb gain (182 to 189) over six to twelve months with no diet change, and with a drop in energy and motivation — he moved to night dosing to manage it. Sleep badly disrupted for the past six to eight months by the baby.

evidence: No price was ever stated and no offer was presented. The rep deliberately stopped short: "I think it would be the best to touch base again next week when you're going to know what's actually going on and we can take it from there."

The reason was clinical timing, stated explicitly: "when you have MRI next week and it's going to turn out that, okay, you're going to be in surgery in two weeks, that's not enough time to prepare you for" and "I don't see starting just for two weeks and then pausing."
A dated follow-up was booked and the invite sent during the call: 4pm Eastern on Thursday 9 July, two hours after the MRI.
Intent is high and untested by price — the prospect qualified himself unprompted on why he needs a coach, and volunteered that he would raise exercise with his surgeon on 13 July.
Counter-evidence: if the surgery is scheduled within weeks, the rep has already said he would not start him, so this may convert to a months-out revisit rather than a near-term sale.
outcome.next_step: Follow-up call at 4pm Eastern on Thursday 9 July, immediately after the 2pm MRI; invite already sent. Prospect also sees his orthopedic surgeon on Monday 13 July and intends to ask specifically about exercise.

notable.note: The counterexample in this batch, and it should be read alongside the rest. Facing a prospect with high intent, a stated pain, no price resistance and a surgical diagnosis two days old, the rep declined to present an offer and booked a follow-up for after the MRI instead. That is the clinically correct decision and it is the only time in twelve files anyone in this corpus slows down for a medical reason. Two things sit against it. First, no clinical clearance was sought for the interim either — it was the prospect, not the rep, who said "I've actually got a follow up with my orthopedic surgeon on Monday the 13th after the MRI, so I can also ask him about exercise too." Second, the rep volunteered a story about a prior prospect with stage-three cancer who came to the programme between radiotherapy and chemotherapy, offered as motivational contrast, which discloses a third party's medical situation and simultaneously evidences the pattern this audit exists to find. The injury-pause policy was also restated here consistently with the Alex call: "when someone gets on board and starts working with Trevor, and something happens, for example, he gets injured, we pause the subscription."
